title: Link-Free Multi-Node Timing Synchronization for Scalable Quantum Networking
authors: Jacob E. Humberd, Mohmad Junaid Ul Haq, Angel Fraire Estrada, Ike Deitch, Tian Li
abstract: Precise timing synchronization is essential for distributed quantum networking, enabling entanglement distribution, quantum teleportation, and entanglement swapping across remote nodes. Existing synchronization architectures rely on dedicated timing-distribution infrastructure, most notably White Rabbit networks, which constrain topology, scalability, and deployment in free-space and satellite environments. Here we demonstrate link-free synchronization of quantum network nodes using independently operating miniature rubidium atomic clocks and computational post-processing. We validate the approach on a deployed metropolitan-scale telecom fiber network spanning three geographically separated nodes. Following drift correction, atomic-clock-based synchronization achieves timing performance approaching that of a White Rabbit benchmark and remains stable over continuous 8-hour operation. As a stringent test of quantum-network functionality, we observe Hong-Ou-Mandel interference across spatially separated nodes with visibility exceeding 70%, statistically equivalent to that obtained using dedicated White Rabbit timing links. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first observation of quantum interference across a deployed metropolitan-scale telecom fiber network synchronized entirely without dedicated timing-transfer infrastructure. These results establish atomic-clock-based synchronization as a scalable, topology-independent alternative to conventional timing-distribution architectures and a practical pathway toward terrestrial, airborne, and space-based quantum networks where dedicated timing links are unavailable.
summary: This work presents a novel method to synchronize remote quantum nodes using only independent miniature atomic clocks rather than dedicated timing links. By applying advanced computational post-processing techniques, the authors achieved timing stability comparable to state-of-the-art systems. This breakthrough establishes a scalable and topology-independent pathway for building large-scale quantum networks.
main_problem: Achieving precise timing synchronization for distributed quantum networking nodes without relying on dedicated, infrastructure-heavy timing distribution links.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated high-visibility Hong-Ou-Mandel interference across a metropolitan-scale fiber network using only independently operating atomic clocks and computational post-processing, matching benchmarks set by White Rabbit systems.
method: They employed a two-stage coincidence peak search algorithm combined with piecewise linear drift compensation applied to raw time-tagging data from miniature rubidium atomic clocks (MACs).
model_or_system: The experiment utilized a deployed metropolitan-scale telecom fiber network connecting three nodes, using MACs as the primary timing reference source for quantum state distribution.
key_observables: Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) interference visibility, coincidence peak Full Width at Half Maximum (FWHM), and timing stability over 8 hours.
important_parameters: Metropolitan scale deployment; rubidium atomic clock precision; $70\%$ HOM visibility threshold; $	ext{sub-nanosecond}$ timing performance goal.
main_assumptions: The residual frequency drift between independent MACs is slow and deterministic enough to be accurately modeled and corrected via post-processing algorithms.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the two-stage coincidence peak identification algorithm (coarse vs. fine search) and compare HOM visibility/FWHM performance across WRS, uncorrected MAC, and drift-corrected MAC in both lab and deployed settings.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first defining the synchronization challenge, detailing the computational method for handling large time offsets, validating the technique on local fiber spools (comparing FWHM), and culminating in the primary demonstration of high-visibility quantum interference across a real, deployed metropolitan network.
why_interesting: It provides an experimental blueprint for realizing scalable quantum networks by circumventing major infrastructure bottlenecks associated with timing distribution, which is crucial for future terrestrial and space-based quantum communication protocols.

(a) A coarse search using temporally subsampled timestamp streams and a 10 ns time-bin width localizes the approximate position of the coincidence peak. (b) The full timestamp records are then analyzed in the vicinity of the iden- tified peak using a 10 ps time-bin width to reconstruct the high-resolution g(2)(τ) distribution. The solid pink line denotes a Gaussian fit to the measured correlation profile.

Fig. 2: Local experimental configurations at UTC employing 10 km fiber spools for comparison of the syn- chronization performance using (a) WRS-based and (b) MAC-based method. (c) Measured coincidence peak FWHM as a function of acquisition time over an 8-hour measurement session using WRS (pink), uncorrected MACs (blue), and drift-corrected MACs (green). The coincidences were sampled at 10-minute intervals, with each data point corresponding to a 60-second integration period.
